# `C#` Attribute 

::: {.callout-note appearance="default" collapse="false"}
C# attribute vs Python decorators
:::

While C# **Attributes** and Python **Decorators** might look similar syntactically (both appearing above methods/classes with special syntax), they work quite differently. Let me explain the key differences and show you how each works.


## Python Decorators vs C# Attributes


### Python Decorators: Runtime Behavior Modification

Python decorators are **functions that wrap other functions**, modifying their behavior at runtime:

```python
def timer_decorator(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        import time
        start = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)  # Call original function
        end = time.time()
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {end - start} seconds")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer_decorator
def slow_function():
    import time
    time.sleep(1)
    return "Done"

slow_function()  # Automatically prints timing info
```


### C# Attributes: Metadata Annotation

C# Attributes are **metadata** attached to code elements. They don't automatically modify behavior - they're just information that can be inspected via reflection:

```csharp
// Define a custom attribute
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method)]
public class TimerAttribute : Attribute
{
    public string Description { get; set; }
    public TimerAttribute(string description = "")
    {
        Description = description;
    }
}

// Apply the attribute
public class MyClass
{
    [Timer("This is a slow operation")]
    public string SlowMethod()
    {
        Thread.Sleep(1000);
        return "Done";
    }
}
```

The attribute above does **nothing** by itself! It's just metadata. To use it, you need to:
1. Use reflection to check if it exists
2. Manually implement the behavior


## Key Differences


```
Python Decorator                    C# Attribute
================                    ============
✓ Modifies behavior directly        ✗ Just metadata
✓ Wraps the function                ✗ Doesn't wrap anything
✓ Executes code before/after        ✗ Requires reflection to use
✓ Runtime modification              ✗ Compile-time metadata
```


## How to Achieve Decorator-like Behavior in C#


### Option 1: Manual Reflection Check

```csharp
public class TimerHelper
{
    public static void ExecuteWithTiming(object instance, string methodName)
    {
        var method = instance.GetType().GetMethod(methodName);
        var hasTimer = method?.GetCustomAttribute<TimerAttribute>() != null;
        
        if (hasTimer)
        {
            var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
            method.Invoke(instance, null);
            stopwatch.Stop();
            Console.WriteLine($"{methodName} took {stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds}ms");
        }
        else
        {
            method?.Invoke(instance, null);
        }
    }
}
```


### Option 2: Using Interceptors (Advanced)

For true decorator-like behavior, you'd need:

- **AOP frameworks** (like PostSharp, Castle Windsor)
- **Source generators** (C# 9+)
- **Middleware patterns** (in ASP.NET Core)

Example with ASP.NET Core Action Filters (which use attributes):

```csharp
public class TimingActionFilter : ActionFilterAttribute
{
    private Stopwatch _stopwatch;
    
    public override void OnActionExecuting(ActionExecutingContext context)
    {
        _stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    }
    
    public override void OnActionExecuted(ActionExecutedContext context)
    {
        _stopwatch.Stop();
        Console.WriteLine($"Action took {_stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds}ms");
    }
}

// In controller:
[TimingActionFilter]
public IActionResult MyAction()
{
    // This WILL be timed automatically!
    return Ok();
}
```


## Common Built-in Attributes in C#


Here are some attributes you'll encounter frequently:

```csharp
// Serialization
[Serializable]
public class Person { }

// JSON serialization
[JsonProperty("user_name")]
public string UserName { get; set; }

// Validation
[Required]
[StringLength(100)]
public string Name { get; set; }

// Unit testing
[Test]
public void TestMethod() { }

// Obsolete warning
[Obsolete("Use NewMethod instead")]
public void OldMethod() { }

// Conditional compilation
[Conditional("DEBUG")]
public void DebugOnly() { }
```
